subject: ela
intro: Every item below includes the full passage it asks about. Read each passage closely, then reason from the author's word choice, tone, and choice of details to the author's purpose or point of view. The author's attitude is usually shown rather than stated outright, so look for the evidence that gives it away.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

"Some people call the daily walk to school a chore. They are wrong. Each morning my students arrive with rosy cheeks, clearer heads, and a hunger to learn that no bus ride ever delivered. Walking wakes the body and the brain. By the time these children reach their desks, they have already breathed fresh air, traded a few jokes, and shaken off the sleepiness that fogs a long car ride. A short walk is not a burden the school forces on families. It is a quiet gift."

What is the author's point of view about walking to school, and which words in the passage convey it? Explain how the word choice reveals the stance.
items.answer: The author strongly favors walking to school and sees it as beneficial, not a hardship. Positive, glowing word choices such as "rosy cheeks," "clearer heads," "hunger to learn," and especially "a quiet gift" carry warm, approving feelings. By calling the walk a "gift" rather than a "chore" or "burden," the author reveals an admiring, supportive attitude toward walking.

steps: Identify what the author feels about the topic, not just the topic itself. The topic is walking to school; the point of view is the author's attitude toward it.
Notice the author directly rejects the negative label: "Some people call the daily walk to school a chore. They are wrong." This signals the author takes a side.
Collect the loaded, positive language: "rosy cheeks," "clearer heads," "hunger to learn," and the closing "a quiet gift." These words carry warm, approving feelings.
Contrast that language with the negative words the author refuses to accept: "chore" and "burden." Choosing "gift" instead shows approval.
Conclude that the author's point of view is clearly in favor of walking, and the warm word choice is the evidence that reveals it.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

"The new arena will seat eighteen thousand fans and open next fall. Backers promise it will bring concerts and jobs to downtown. They rarely mention the four hundred families who will lose their homes to make room for the parking, or the traffic that will choke these quiet streets every game night. The city found money for luxury seating but somehow none for the bus lines those families depend on. Progress, it seems, has a habit of arriving for some and rolling right over others."

Is the author neutral about the new arena, or does the author take a side? Use evidence from the passage to explain.
items.answer: The author is not neutral and is critical of the arena project. Evidence includes the focus on "four hundred families who will lose their homes," the contrast that the city "found money for luxury seating but somehow none for the bus lines," and the closing line that progress "rolling right over" some people. These details and the bitter tone show the author opposes the project as unfair.

steps: Check whether the passage presents both sides evenly or leans one way. It mentions the backers' promises only briefly, then spends most of its space on the costs.
Notice the selection of details: the author emphasizes lost homes, choked traffic, and cut bus lines, which are all downsides.
Spot the loaded contrast: money for "luxury seating but somehow none" for buses. The word "somehow" hints the author finds this unfair.
Read the closing image of progress "rolling right over others." That negative metaphor reveals the author's disapproval.
Conclude the author takes a side against the arena, so calling the passage neutral would miss the one-sided detail selection and critical tone.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

"A solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes directly between the Sun and Earth, casting its shadow on our planet. During a total eclipse, the Moon blocks the Sun completely for a few minutes, and the sky darkens as if night has fallen. Scientists can predict eclipses years in advance because the movements of the Moon and Earth follow regular patterns. People should never look directly at the Sun during an eclipse without special protective glasses, because the bright light can damage the eyes."

What is the author's main purpose in writing this passage? Explain how you can tell, using evidence from the text.
items.answer: The author's purpose is to inform readers about how a solar eclipse works and how to view one safely. The passage explains the cause of eclipses, describes what happens during one, and gives a safety fact, all in plain, factual language with no opinion words. The neutral, explanatory tone and the focus on facts show the purpose is to inform and explain rather than to persuade.

steps: Ask why the author wrote this: to inform, persuade, warn, entertain, or call to act.
Look at the content: it defines an eclipse, describes a total eclipse, and explains why scientists can predict them. These are facts, not opinions.
Check the language for loaded or opinion words. There are none; the tone is neutral and explanatory.
Note the one safety statement uses the word "should," but it gives factual safety guidance rather than arguing a position or taking a side.
Conclude the purpose is to inform and explain, supported by the factual content and neutral tone.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

"Owners brag that their gleaming new phones can do almost anything. What they forget to mention is the mountain of dead phones piling up behind the shine. Every year people toss out millions of working devices just to chase the latest model. These discarded phones leak harmful metals into the soil, and the rush to replace them keeps factories burning through energy and minerals at a furious pace. We treat these gadgets as if they were disposable. They are not."

Which phrase in the passage most clearly reveals the author's attitude toward replacing phones every year, and what attitude does it show?
items.answer: Phrases such as "the mountain of dead phones piling up behind the shine," "chase the latest model," and "leak harmful metals" most clearly reveal the author's attitude. They show a critical, disapproving attitude toward replacing phones every year, because the author frames the habit as wasteful and harmful rather than describing it neutrally.

steps: Separate neutral facts from phrases that carry feeling. "Millions of working devices" is closer to a fact; the imagery around it carries opinion.
Find the most loaded language: "mountain of dead phones piling up behind the shine" and "chase the latest model" both sound disapproving.
Note words with negative connotations: "harmful metals," "furious pace," and the blunt closing "They are not."
Decide what attitude these reveal: the author treats yearly replacement as wasteful and damaging, a critical stance.
Avoid picking a neutral detail, such as the number of phones, since that fact alone does not carry the author's feeling.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

"The town is debating whether to keep the old library open. Supporters argue that some will say the building is outdated and the books can all be found online. That argument sounds modern, but it forgets the children who have no computer at home, the seniors who come for company, and the quiet readers who have nowhere else to go. A library is not just a shelf of books. It is the one free room in town where everyone is welcome."

The author mentions the argument that the library is "outdated" and that books "can all be found online." Does the author agree with that argument? Explain how the way the author handles it reveals the author's own point of view.
items.answer: No, the author does not agree with that argument. The author raises the "outdated" and "books online" argument only to knock it down, saying it "forgets" the children, seniors, and quiet readers who depend on the library. By dismissing the opposing view and praising the library as "the one free room in town where everyone is welcome," the author reveals a point of view firmly in favor of keeping the library open.

steps: Identify the opposing view in the passage: that the library is outdated and books are all online.
Notice the author introduces it with "some will say" and "that argument sounds modern, but," which sets it up to be challenged.
See how the author handles it: the word "forgets" signals the author thinks the argument leaves out important things, namely the people who need the library.
Read the closing praise of the library as "the one free room in town where everyone is welcome," which shows the author's own warm stance.
Conclude the author disagrees with the opposing view and supports keeping the library, so treating the counterargument as the author's position would be a mistake.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

"For years our school has let students choose between art and music in sixth grade. Now the board wants to drop both and add another hour of test review. Picture it: a building where no one paints, no one sings, and every period sounds the same. Test scores may tick up a point or two, but at what cost? We will have traded the spark in a child's eye for a slightly higher number on a chart. Surely our children are worth more than that."

What is the author's purpose in writing this passage, and how is that purpose conveyed? Use evidence from the text.
items.answer: The author's purpose is to persuade readers to oppose dropping art and music in favor of test review. The purpose is conveyed through the vivid negative picture of a school where "no one paints, no one sings," the rhetorical question "at what cost?", the contrast between "the spark in a child's eye" and "a slightly higher number on a chart," and the closing appeal "Surely our children are worth more than that." These persuasive choices push readers to take the author's side.

steps: Decide why the author wrote this. It is not just describing a policy; it argues against one.
Find the persuasive devices: the imagined scene of a school with "no one paints, no one sings" makes the change sound bleak.
Notice the rhetorical question "at what cost?" and the value contrast between "the spark in a child's eye" and "a slightly higher number on a chart."
Read the closing appeal to the reader: "Surely our children are worth more than that." This urges agreement.
Conclude the purpose is to persuade readers to oppose the change, conveyed through emotional imagery, a rhetorical question, and a direct appeal.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

"Honeybees are vanishing from farms across the country, and the trend should worry everyone, not just beekeepers. One out of every three bites of food we eat depends on these insects to pollinate the crops. When a hive collapses, fewer apples grow, fewer almonds ripen, and prices climb at the store. Scientists point to pesticides and lost habitat as causes we created and can still fix. The bees are sending us a warning. The question is whether we will listen."

The topic of this passage is honeybees. What is the difference between the author's purpose and the author's point of view in this passage? Explain both.
items.answer: The author's purpose is to warn readers about the disappearance of honeybees and to call them to act. The author's point of view is that the bee decline is a serious, urgent problem that humans caused and can fix. The purpose is what the author is trying to do (warn and prompt action), while the point of view is the author's concerned, alarmed attitude toward the topic, shown by phrases like "should worry everyone" and "sending us a warning."

steps: Separate the three ideas: the topic is honeybees, the purpose is why the author wrote it, and the point of view is how the author feels about it.
Determine the purpose by looking at what the author wants the reader to do: "should worry everyone" and "whether we will listen" aim to warn and move readers to act.
Determine the point of view by looking at the author's attitude: words like "vanishing," "worry," and "warning" show concern and urgency.
State the difference clearly: purpose is the goal (warn and call to act), point of view is the stance (the decline is serious and fixable).
Avoid the trap of naming the topic, honeybees, as either the purpose or the point of view.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

"The city installed its first round of electric scooters this spring, and residents have had plenty to say. Riders praise the scooters as a quick, cheap way to cross town without a car. Critics counter that the devices clutter sidewalks and create hazards for people on foot. City data shows trips have climbed steadily each week, while complaints to the council have also risen. The council plans to review both the ridership numbers and the safety reports before deciding whether to expand the program."

Is the author taking a side for or against the scooters, or presenting the issue neutrally? Explain your answer using evidence from the passage.
items.answer: The author is presenting the issue neutrally and does not take a side. The passage gives the riders' praise and the critics' concerns in balanced, even amounts, reports facts from "city data" about both rising trips and rising complaints, and ends by stating the council will "review both" before deciding. The fair, factual language with no loaded words shows the author is staying neutral.

steps: Check whether the passage leans toward one side or balances both.
Notice it presents praise ("quick, cheap way") and criticism ("clutter sidewalks and create hazards") in roughly equal measure.
Look at the data sentence: it reports both rising trips and rising complaints, not just the good or the bad.
Read the ending: the council will "review both" sets of information, and the author does not push a verdict.
Conclude the author is neutral here, supported by balanced detail selection and the absence of loaded language.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

"They call it fast fashion, and fast it is. A shirt is designed, sewn, shipped, worn twice, and tossed in the time it takes a real garment to earn its first wrinkle. Stores churn out new styles every week to keep us buying, and we oblige, hauling home armfuls of clothes that fall apart by summer. The bins behind these shops overflow. Somewhere a worker stitches for pennies so we can wear something disposable. This is not a bargain. It is a quiet kind of waste dressed up as a deal."

How does the author's word choice in this passage convey the author's point of view about fast fashion? Identify specific words and explain the attitude they reveal.
items.answer: The author's word choice conveys a critical, disapproving point of view toward fast fashion. Words and phrases such as "tossed," "churn out," "fall apart by summer," "overflow," "stitches for pennies," "disposable," and especially "a quiet kind of waste dressed up as a deal" carry negative, judgmental feelings. They reveal that the author sees fast fashion as wasteful and unfair rather than as a good value.

steps: Recall that point of view is the author's attitude, revealed largely through connotative word choice.
List the loaded words: "tossed," "churn out," "fall apart," "overflow," "stitches for pennies," and "disposable."
Note these words carry negative feelings: cheapness, waste, and unfairness.
Examine the key line: "This is not a bargain. It is a quiet kind of waste dressed up as a deal," which directly states a critical judgment.
Conclude the word choice reveals a disapproving attitude, so a reader who looked only at the topic and missed these words might wrongly call the passage neutral.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

"Marie Curie was born in Poland in 1867 and later moved to Paris to study science. She discovered two new elements, polonium and radium, and her research led to important advances in medicine. In 1903 she became the first woman to win a Nobel Prize, and in 1911 she won a second one in a different field. Curie spent much of her life in a small laboratory, working long hours with little money. Her notebooks are still so radioactive that they are kept in lead-lined boxes."

What is the author's main purpose in this passage, and how can you tell? Use evidence from the text.
items.answer: The author's main purpose is to inform readers about Marie Curie's life and accomplishments. The passage gives factual details about where she was born, what she discovered, the prizes she won, and how she worked, all without opinion words or an argument. The straightforward, factual presentation and neutral tone show the purpose is to inform rather than to persuade or to argue a point.

steps: Ask what the author is trying to do: inform, persuade, warn, or entertain.
Survey the content: birthplace, discoveries, Nobel Prizes, working conditions, and a fact about her notebooks. These are biographical facts.
Check the tone for loaded language or argument. The language is factual and even, with no call to act or opinion stated.
Note that even the striking detail about radioactive notebooks is presented as a fact, not as praise or criticism.
Conclude the purpose is to inform, supported by the factual content and neutral tone.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

"The school wants to push the start of classes back by an hour, and you can already hear the grumbling about changed bus routes and shifted schedules. But look closer. Teenagers are biologically wired to sleep later, and forcing them awake at dawn leaves them foggy through their first classes. Schools that made the switch saw grades rise and absences fall. Yes, adjusting the buses will take effort. A few weeks of inconvenience is a small price for years of rested, focused students."

The author mentions complaints about "changed bus routes and shifted schedules." How does the way the author handles this objection reveal the author's own point of view? Explain.
items.answer: The author raises the objection about bus routes and schedules only to push it aside, treating it as a minor "inconvenience" and "a small price" compared with the benefits. By admitting the objection but quickly outweighing it with evidence that "grades rise and absences fall," the author reveals a point of view in favor of the later start time. The objection is acknowledged, not adopted.

steps: Identify the objection the author raises: complaints about changed bus routes and shifted schedules.
Notice the signal "But look closer," which tells the reader the author is about to argue against the complaint.
See how the author minimizes the objection: "A few weeks of inconvenience is a small price." The author concedes it but treats it as minor.
Note the supporting evidence the author offers for the other side: "grades rise and absences fall."
Conclude the author favors the later start time, so mistaking the objection for the author's own view would misread the passage.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

"There is talk of paving the meadow at the edge of town to build another parking lot. Defenders of the plan say the spaces are needed. Perhaps. But I have watched children chase fireflies across that grass on summer evenings and seen families spread blankets there on the Fourth of July. Asphalt does not hold a picnic. Once the last open field is gone, no amount of parking will give it back. Some things, once paved over, are paved over for good."

What is the author's point of view about paving the meadow, and which details and word choices convey it? Explain.
items.answer: The author is opposed to paving the meadow and values it as an irreplaceable open space. Warm, vivid details such as "children chase fireflies across that grass" and "families spread blankets there on the Fourth of July" make the meadow appealing, while pointed lines like "Asphalt does not hold a picnic" and "once paved over, are paved over for good" warn against the loss. These details and word choices convey the author's protective, disapproving stance toward the plan.

steps: Determine the author's attitude toward the topic of paving the meadow.
Notice the brief, dismissive handling of the other side: "Perhaps," then a turn with "But."
Collect the warm imagery: fireflies, summer evenings, and Fourth of July blankets, which make the meadow precious.
Find the pointed lines that warn of loss: "Asphalt does not hold a picnic" and "paved over for good."
Conclude the author opposes paving the meadow, conveyed through fond details and word choices that stress an irreversible loss.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

"Plastic water bottles are everywhere, and that convenience comes at a steep price. Americans buy tens of billions of them each year, and most end up in landfills or the ocean rather than a recycling bin. The plastic takes centuries to break down, harming wildlife and crumbling into tiny pieces that slip into our water and food. Tap water, by contrast, is cleaner and cheaper than most people assume. Refilling a single sturdy bottle is one of the easiest swaps a person can make. Isn't it time we put down the plastic?"

What is the author's purpose in writing this passage, and how do the author's choices convey it? Use evidence from the text.
items.answer: The author's purpose is to persuade readers to stop using disposable plastic bottles and switch to refillable ones. The author conveys this by stacking up negative facts about plastic ("landfills or the ocean," "harming wildlife," "slip into our water and food"), praising the alternative as "cleaner and cheaper" and "one of the easiest swaps," and ending with the rhetorical question "Isn't it time we put down the plastic?" These persuasive choices push the reader toward action.

steps: Decide what the author wants from the reader. The passage builds a case, so it is more than pure information.
Notice the selection of details all point one way: plastic is wasteful, long-lasting, and harmful.
See the author promote the alternative: tap water is "cleaner and cheaper" and refilling is "one of the easiest swaps."
Read the closing rhetorical question "Isn't it time we put down the plastic?" which nudges the reader to act.
Conclude the purpose is to persuade, conveyed through one-sided detail selection, praise of the alternative, and a closing call to act.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

"The mayor unveiled her budget on Monday, and the reactions arrived almost as fast. The plan adds money for road repairs and after-school programs while trimming the parks department. Council members from the north side welcomed the road funds; those from the south worried about cuts to their neighborhood pool. The mayor said the budget reflects 'hard choices in a tight year.' A public hearing is scheduled for next week, when residents will have a chance to weigh in before the final vote."

Does this passage reveal the author's personal point of view on the budget, or is the author reporting neutrally? Explain using evidence.
items.answer: The author is reporting neutrally and does not reveal a personal point of view on the budget. The passage lays out the plan's additions and cuts, gives both the north side's approval and the south side's worry, quotes the mayor, and notes the upcoming hearing, all in factual language without loaded words. The balanced coverage and even tone show the author is reporting rather than taking a side.

steps: Decide whether the author argues a position or simply reports events.
Notice the passage presents the budget's pluses (road repairs, after-school programs) and minuses (cuts to parks and the pool) without favoring either.
See that both council factions are quoted fairly: north side pleased, south side worried.
Check for loaded language. The tone is even, and the author lets the mayor and council members speak rather than judging them.
Conclude the author is neutral, supported by balanced detail selection and factual, even tone.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

"Zoos like to call themselves arks, safe havens that protect endangered animals. The picture they paint is comforting. Look past the brochures, though, and you find lions pacing the same twenty steps for hours and elephants swaying in place, a behavior they never show in the wild. These animals were built to roam miles each day, not to circle a moat for the amusement of a Saturday crowd. A cage with a painted backdrop is still a cage. We should ask whether our curiosity is worth their confinement."

The author mentions that zoos call themselves "arks" and "safe havens." Does the author accept that description? Explain how the author's treatment of it reveals the author's point of view.
items.answer: No, the author does not accept the description. The author raises the "arks" and "safe havens" image only to challenge it, urging the reader to "look past the brochures" to see lions "pacing" and elephants "swaying in place." By rejecting the comforting picture and arguing "a cage with a painted backdrop is still a cage," the author reveals a critical point of view that opposes keeping animals in zoos. The closing question pushes the reader to question zoos too.

steps: Identify the view the author quotes: zoos as "arks" and "safe havens."
Notice the author signals doubt right away by calling the picture "comforting" and then saying "Look past the brochures, though."
See the contrasting details the author chooses: pacing lions and swaying elephants, which suggest suffering, not safety.
Read the pointed line "A cage with a painted backdrop is still a cage" and the closing question about whether "curiosity is worth their confinement."
Conclude the author rejects the zoos' description and holds a critical point of view, so treating "safe havens" as the author's own view would misread the passage.
